title: Joined or spaced
hookLine: a hashtag with no spaces gets misread; older copies of the Granth run every word together
tomorrow: what's the line of small print above every hymn?

cards: A hashtag with no spaces can be read two ways, and somebody always reads it the wrong way. Now try a whole page like that.

In older hand-written copies of the Granth, the words run on, letter after letter, line after line, with no gaps. That's called larivaar. Many printed copies today put a space between each word; that's called padched.
Same letters, different page. And in a gurdwara, the copy on the high seat may well be the joined one. So which should a reader learn on?

teach.h: FOR LARIVAAR: LEARN WHERE WORDS BREAK.
teach.b: Two real views, each in its own best words. First, the case for larivaar. This is the Granth as it was written and handed down, and there's respect in leaving it whole.
Because the words aren't broken for you, you have to learn where they break, slowly, usually with a teacher. That slowness is the point.
It keeps a reader close to every line, and it keeps any one editor's word breaks from quietly becoming the only reading. Now the case for padched.

teach.h: FOR PADCHED: THE SAME LETTERS, OPEN.
teach.b: The letters are exactly the same; nothing is added but space. And space opens the page to anyone who can read Gurmukhi, at home, on a phone, with no teacher nearby.
Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase, that the teaching is shared by everyone, people of every class alike. A spaced page puts that sharing into practice.
Some families keep both: a larivaar copy where the Guru is formally seated, a spaced gutka or app for every day. Neither side wants the words changed. Neither wants them rushed.

teach.h: EITHER WAY, ONE WORD AT A TIME.
teach.b: And here's what they share, which is today's line: whichever copy is open, the Guru's words are read word by word.
Run them together carelessly and a line can blur into something it never said. Take them one at a time and they land.

how: Some gurdwaras seat a larivaar copy of the Guru Granth Sahib for the main reading, and readers learn its word breaks through santhiaa with a teacher; many Sikhs read daily from spaced (padched) gutkas, printed copies or apps.

o: a hymn that is sung without music
a gurdwara's main reader of the Granth
the Granth written with its words joined

games.q: word by word — tap the pairs.

games.q: your dad says learn on the spaced app. your grandmother says learn the joined copy, like the one at the gurdwara. you lean toward the app. what's her best case?
o: older copies are holier, so the spaced ones don't really count.
joined words make you learn where each word breaks, slowly, with a teacher, and that slowness keeps you close.
spaced copies quietly change some of the Guru's letters.
games.why: the strongest case for larivaar isn't that spaced copies are wrong: the letters match. it's that learning the breaks yourself keeps you close to every line.

practice: Choose one short line, from the Japji or any page you have. Say it out loud slowly, one word on each breath out, with a full pause between the words.
If your copy is spaced, let the gaps set the pace; if it's joined, let your breath find the breaks.

wordCard.voice: Larivaar: a copy of the Granth with the words written joined, no spaces between them, as in older hand-written copies. The fifth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: larivaar, the words of the Granth written joined, with no spaces.

carryVoice: Your line: word by word. Joined or spaced, that's how the Guru's words are read. See you tomorrow.
